lines.text: Calibration maths. The robot is parked exactly on the scoring spot. Its wheels say four, one, facing zero.
Tag to goal, run backwards, is the trip from robot to tag. So the tag must be at four point six, one, facing back.
After backing off thirty centimeters, the tag should appear zero point nine meters straight ahead, facing the robot.
A camera turned one degree reports zero point eight nine six four, minus zero point zero one one three, one seventy nine: a centimeter off.
We want a fix, A, so that A composed with measured equals expected. Undo measured on both sides: A equals expected, composed with measured inverse.
Here A is three and a half millimeters, minus four point three millimeters, and one degree. The one degree undoes the camera's turn.
Work it out anywhere along the back-off: A comes out the same. A flat line is what a good calibration log looks like.
A is averaged over every photo. Angles use sine and cosine, so one seventy nine and minus one seventy nine average to one eighty, not zero.
Then every photo from that camera gets the same fix: A, composed with measured.
It absorbs the camera's mounting error, the solve's yaw bias at those distances, and small lens errors.
But it also absorbs any parking mistake, and the calibration tag's own error. So park with a jig, on a well-built element.
